questions.q: You observe 'Diagonal Cracks' (45-degree angle) near the support of a heavily loaded beam. What does this indicate, and what is the immediate remedy?
o: Torsional Failure; increase the width of the beam to resist twisting.
Shrinkage Cracking; apply a high-strength epoxy injection to seal the cracks.
Flexural Failure; apply carbon fiber wrap to the bottom of the beam.
Shear Failure (Diagonal Tension); provide shoring and consult a structural engineer for reinforcement.
questions.n: Diagonal cracks near supports are classic signs of shear stress exceeding the concrete's capacity, requiring immediate temporary support and professional intervention.

questions.q: What is 'Creep' in concrete, and why should an architect care about it in long-span beams?
o: Chemical erosion of rebar; to prevent the structural failure of the beam over time.
Long-term deformation under constant load; to prevent crushing of partitions, glass, and doors below.
Thermal expansion; to allow for the installation of expansion joints in the middle of the span.
Instantaneous deflection; to ensure the beam doesn't snap during the removal of forms.
questions.n: Creep causes gradual sagging over years, which can put unintended pressure on non-structural elements installed beneath the beam.

questions.q: Why is a 'Short Column' effect dangerous during an earthquake?
o: It attracts disproportionately higher shear forces, leading to brittle, explosive failure.
It creates a 'Soft Story' at the base, leading to the pancake collapse of the building.
It is too flexible, causing the building to sway excessively and hit adjacent structures.
It has less concrete volume, making it easier to crumble under vertical pressure.
questions.n: Because stiffness is inversely proportional to the cube of the height, shorter columns take on more force than they can dissipate, leading to sudden failure.

questions.q: In a residential floor, what is the difference between a Dead Load and a Live Load?
o:
There is no difference; they are both calculated using the same safety factor of 
1.4
1.4.
Dead Load includes wind and seismic forces; Live Load is the weight of the concrete slabs.
Dead Load is the weight of people; Live Load is the weight of the furniture.
Dead Load is the building's own weight; Live Load is the weight of movable objects and occupants.
questions.n: Dead loads are constant (structure, walls, finishes), while live loads are transient (people, furniture, equipment).

questions.q: What is 'Pinching' in a beam-column joint during a seismic event?
o: Degradation of the bond between rebar and concrete, reducing the joint's load-carrying ability.
The narrowing of the column width due to extreme vertical compression.
The physical contact between two adjacent buildings during a quake.
The crushing of the floor slab where it meets the vertical face of the column.
questions.n: Repeated cycling causes the concrete to lose its grip on the steel, resulting in a 'pinched' hysteresis loop and reduced energy dissipation.

questions.q: What is the difference between TLA (Total Lot Area) and AMBF (Allowable Maximum Building Footprint)?
o: TLA is the buildable area; AMBF is the total area including the sidewalk.
TLA is the whole property; AMBF is the allowed ground area after deducting setbacks and yards.
TLA is used for commercial lots; AMBF is used only for residential lots.
TLA is the floor area of the building; AMBF is the area of the yard.
questions.n: The AMBF represents the maximum 'footprint' or horizontal projection of the building on the ground level.

questions.q: Under NBC, what is a 'Court' and why is it required for some buildings?
o: The area between the sidewalk and the building facade used for parking.
An unoccupied space used to provide natural light and ventilation to inner rooms.
An outdoor area reserved for sports activities in residential condominiums.
A specialized room for legal proceedings; required for government buildings.
questions.n: Courts ensure that rooms not adjacent to the street or yards still receive the minimum legal requirements for air and light.

questions.q: What is the 'Angle of Departure' in the context of building height limits?
o: The maximum angle of a ramp for PWD accessibility.
An imaginary line from the center of the RROW that limits the height of the facade.
The angle at which an airplane must climb to avoid hitting the building.
The slope of the roof required to ensure proper drainage of rainwater.
questions.n: This rule ensures that buildings don't cast excessive shadows or block all air from reaching the street level.

questions.q: A contractor offers you a 'Commission' (kickback) for specifying their brand of tiles. Why is this a violation of the Code of Ethics?
o: It is only a violation if the client finds out; if kept secret, it is considered a 'professional bonus'.
It creates a Conflict of Interest and compromises the architect's impartiality.
Because tiles are not structural, so the commission should be for steel or concrete instead.
Because the commission is usually too small to be worth the risk.
questions.n: The architect's duty is to recommend the best product for the client's needs, which cannot be done if the architect is financially incentivized by a supplier.

questions.q: You find out another architect is already working on a project, but the client wants to hire you instead. What is your first step?
o: Offer a lower fee than the first architect to secure the contract.
Ignore the situation; as long as the client pays you, the previous architect is not your concern.
Accept the project immediately to prevent the client from changing their mind.
Formally communicate with the first architect to confirm legal termination and fee settlement.
questions.n: This ensures that you are not 'supplanting' a colleague and that the client has fulfilled their legal obligations to the previous professional.

questions.q: Can an architect be the Owner of a construction company that builds the projects they designed?
o: Yes, but they can only charge for construction and must provide the design for free.
No, an architect must always remain an independent consultant and never touch construction.
No, this is strictly forbidden by RA 9266 to prevent monopolies.
Yes, provided roles are clearly separated in contracts and disclosed in writing to the client.
questions.n: Full disclosure and separate legal agreements prevent conflicts of interest and ensure the client understands the dual role.

questions.q: What is 'Unfair Competition' in architecture?
o: Designing a building that is more beautiful than the one next door.
Under-cutting fees or using 'free' schematic designs to win a project.
Hiring employees from a rival architectural firm by offering higher salaries.
Participating in an international design competition without a local partner.
questions.n: These practices devalue the profession and create an uneven playing field based on financial sacrifice rather than merit.

questions.q: If a Client asks you to sign and seal a set of plans you did not prepare or supervise, what should you do?
o: Sign them but charge double the usual fee to cover the risk.
Sign them only if the client signs a waiver absolving you of any structural responsibility.
Refuse; this is 'Dry-sealing,' a criminal violation that can lead to license revocation.
Review the plans for 10 minutes, then sign them to satisfy the supervision requirement.
questions.n: An architect's seal is a guarantee of personal preparation or direct supervision; violating this is a major legal offense under RA 9266.

questions.q: Why do we place 'Expansion Joints' in long concrete walls or large floor slabs?
o: To provide a place for electrical conduits to run between rooms.
To make the building look like it is made of separate modular blocks.
To reduce the amount of concrete needed, thereby saving on material costs.
To allow for thermal expansion and contraction without cracking the structure.
questions.n: Expansion joints act as pre-planned gaps that accommodate the natural movement of materials due to temperature changes.

questions.q: In high-rise plumbing, what is a 'Water Hammer' and how do you prevent it?
o: The sound of air escaping the pipes; prevented by increasing water pressure.
A thud caused by sudden water flow stop; prevented by installing Air Chambers.
A tool used by plumbers to fix pipes; prevented by using better tools.
The vibration of the pump; prevented by using rubber mounts.
questions.n: Air chambers provide a cushion of air that absorbs the momentum of the water when a valve is closed quickly.

questions.q: Why is 'Marine Plywood' used for formworks instead of ordinary plywood?
o: It uses waterproof glue (WBP) to prevent delamination when in contact with wet concrete.
Because it is naturally fireproof and prevents site accidents.
It has a smoother surface that makes the concrete look like marble.
Because it is cheaper and easier to find on construction sites.
questions.n: Ordinary plywood would peel apart (delaminate) when exposed to the moisture of wet concrete and humidity.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Priming' a wall before painting?
o: To seal the surface, improve adhesion, and prevent alkalinity from bleaching the paint.
To make the wall appear thicker and more solid.
To allow the paint to be easily washed off if the client dislikes the color.
To hide the mistakes of the mason who plastered the wall.
questions.n: Primers provide a stable, neutral base that ensures the final paint layer sticks well and stays true to its color.
